claims.text: The target system is bulk, high-purity, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with negligible extrinsic defects.
A predictive framework can decouple lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-size and bond-length variations produce local lattice distortions in solid-solution HEAs.
Static bond-length disorder and dynamic thermal distortions can be represented jointly through an effective-temperature scaling parameter.
The effective-temperature framework captures force-constant fluctuations caused by bonding variations.
Static and dynamic lattice distortions shorten phonon lifetimes in HfNbTaTiZr.
The shortened phonon lifetimes reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic transport in a refractory HEA can be modeled using electronic parameters including plasma frequency, free-electron density, and terahertz-derived relaxation time.
Ab initio-based or machine-learning-enhanced electronic models provide a separately validated description of charge-carrier heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The lattice thermal conductivity of defect-free HfNbTaTiZr will be nearly temperature invariant from 200 K to 1200 K.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be approximately 30–50% below conventional Debye-based estimates.
The electronic thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr will increase linearly with temperature from 200 K to 1200 K.
Separately treating lattice and electronic transport will improve the accuracy of total thermal-conductivity predictions.
Conventional Debye-based approaches combine or conflate lattice and electronic contributions and fail to resolve relevant atomic-scale disorder.
The 30–50% reduction estimate follows from scaling laws observed in related HEAs.
Terahertz spectroscopy can supply information relevant to electronic conduction in refractory HEAs.
Time-domain thermoreflectance can independently quantify the lattice contribution over the proposed 200–1200 K range.
Extrinsic defects, impurities, or phase segregation may cause deviations from the prediction, and the prediction is not asserted outside 200–1200 K.
Failure of either lattice-conductivity invariance, the 30–50% reduction, or the linear electronic trend would falsify or require reconsideration of the model.
